nameStory: The "spiny oak slug" gets its name from the caterpillar's bizarre appearance - it looks more like a colorful, spiny sea slug than any caterpillar you've ever seen! The spines aren't just for show either; they deliver a painful sting if you touch them. The "oak" part comes from this caterpillar's favorite dining spots - oak leaves, though it's not picky and will munch on many other trees too.
description: The Spiny Oak-slug Moth is most famous for its extraordinary caterpillar stage, which looks like nothing else you'll find crawling around New England. Instead of the typical fuzzy or smooth caterpillar body, this larva resembles a tiny, flattened cushion decorated with colorful spines that stick out like a punk rocker's mohawk. The caterpillar is typically bright green or yellow-green with distinctive red, orange, or purple spiny projections. The adult moth, by contrast, is a modest brown creature that most people would overlook completely.

idTips.label: Slug-like body shape
idTips.description: The caterpillar has a flattened, oval body that hugs close to leaves, completely unlike typical cylindrical caterpillars - it truly looks like a colorful sea slug that somehow ended up on a tree

idTips.label: Stinging spines
idTips.description: Clusters of branched, colorful spines protrude from the body - DO NOT TOUCH as they deliver a painful, nettle-like sting that can cause welts and burning sensations

idTips.label: Bright coloration
idTips.description: Base color is usually bright lime green or yellow-green, with spines that can be red, orange, purple, or yellow - the colors are so vivid they almost look artificial

idTips.label: Size and movement
idTips.description: About the size of a large grape when mature, moves very slowly and deliberately across leaf surfaces with a gliding motion rather than the typical caterpillar crawl

idTips.label: Feeding damage
idTips.description: Creates irregular holes in leaves, often feeding from the underside first, leaving translucent windows in the leaf before eating through completely

habitat: Found throughout New England's deciduous forests, especially where oak trees grow, but also common in mixed woodlands, parks, and suburban areas with mature trees. Look for them on oak, cherry, apple, maple, and many other broadleaf trees and shrubs. They prefer the middle to upper canopy but can be found on lower branches and young trees.

seasonality.spring: Adult moths emerge and begin laying eggs on host plants. Eggs are small, round, and often laid singly on leaf undersides.
seasonality.summer: Peak caterpillar season - this is when you're most likely to spot the distinctive spiny larvae feeding on leaves, typically from July through early September.
seasonality.fall: Late-stage caterpillars may still be visible in early fall before pupating in the leaf litter, creating brown cocoons among fallen leaves.
seasonality.winter: Pupae overwinter in cocoons hidden in leaf litter and soil. Adult moths and caterpillars are not visible during this dormant period.

funFact: Despite looking like a creature from another planet, this caterpillar's stinging spines contain the same type of venom found in stinging nettles - but concentrated into tiny hypodermic needles that can pierce right through thin gloves!
confusionNotes: The caterpillar is so unique it's rarely confused with anything else in New England - no other caterpillar has that flat, slug-like body with prominent stinging spines. The adult moth, however, is easily overlooked among other small brown moths, but the caterpillar stage is unmistakable.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that some moth caterpillars can sting! This is one of several "slug caterpillar" species that pack a painful punch, so the golden rule is: never touch a caterpillar you can't identify, especially colorful, spiny ones.
compareHints: This is the only Euclea species regularly found in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Among other slug caterpillars in the region, it's distinguished by its specific combination of bright green base color and prominent branched spines - other stinging caterpillars like the saddleback caterpillar have different color patterns and spine arrangements.
